performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: The Story of the Kalender Prince is the second movement of Scheherazade, Op. 35. Scheherazade’s violin introduces the bassoon, whose winding melody in B minor passes to the oboe and strings, and brass fanfares interrupt it repeatedly.

sections.label: Frame · Violin and harp return
sections.mNote: The violin plays Scheherazade’s recitative again.

sections.label: A · Bassoon solo over muted double basses
sections.mNote: Four double basses play beneath the bassoon solo.

sections.label: B · Brass fanfares interrupt
sections.mNote: Short calls replace the long woodwind phrases.

sections.label: Link · Clarinet and plucked strings
sections.mNote: A free clarinet solo over soft repeated string chords.

sections.label: Dev · Brass march, expanded
sections.mNote: Piccolo and percussion join the orchestral march.

sections.label: A′ · Bassoon theme returns
sections.mNote: A bassoon cadenza restates the opening melody.

sections.label: A″ · Kalender theme, full orchestra
sections.mNote: Winds and strings take up the bassoon’s melody.

sections.label: Coda · Wind phrases, then B major
sections.mNote: The final Animato moves to the major chord.

cues.title: Solo violin recitative
cues.text: The solo violin plays another recitative over harp chords, marked Lento, Recitativo. The theme is Scheherazade’s, heard in the first movement. The violin cadenza slows with a ritardando, and the bassoon takes over as soloist.
cues.evidence: Full score, second movement, printed pp. 24–25: Lento, Recitativo, violin cadenza and ritardando before the bassoon. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bassoon solo in B minor
cues.text: A bassoon begins in B minor, marked dolce ed espressivo, sweetly and expressively. Four muted double basses hold a quiet foundation beneath it. The tune alternates short dance figures with longer held notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 25: Andantino, bassoon marked Capriccioso, quasi recitando and dolce ed espressivo; four solo double basses, con sordino. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Naoum Blinder, solo violin
cues.text: The solo violin is Naoum Blinder, concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony. He reached the United States in 1928 with the banker Felix Warburg’s sponsorship and taught many violinists, Isaac Stern among them.
cues.evidence: Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary of Naoum Blinder: former concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony, teacher of Isaac Stern, in the United States from 1928 under Felix Warburg’s sponsorship. https://www.jta.org/archive/naoum-blinder-teacher-of-many-ranking-musicians-dies-in-san-francisco

cues.title: Variations on the bassoon theme
cues.text: The bassoon’s theme returns several times, each time with a different orchestration. The strings play tremolo, a repeated accompaniment figure runs beneath the theme, and short, sharp figures cut across the texture.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the movement as a kaleidoscope of variations with string tremolandos, thrummings and pricking textures. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Conservatory professorship, 1871
cues.text: In 1871 the composer accepted a professorship at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory. He was twenty-seven. Alongside his teaching, he set about learning the harmony and counterpoint that his own training had left out.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard gives the appointment and age; Paul Serotsky describes the subsequent self-education. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement ; https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm

cues.title: Brass calls and march
cues.text: Short, loud brass calls interrupt the long melody. The new idea comes from the Sultan’s phrase in the first movement, and horns, trumpets and trombones develop it into a march.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 30–31; Serotsky identifies the central idea’s relation to the Sultan’s motto and its development into a march. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Sultan’s theme in the brass
cues.text: The unison phrase associated with the Sultan at the opening of the suite returns in the brass in this movement. Rimsky-Korsakov wrote that it serves here only as musical material, since in the Kalender’s tale “there cannot, however, be any mention of Sultan Shakhriar.”
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, pp. 247–248. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Clarinet solo over pizzicato strings
cues.text: A solo clarinet plays the tune freely, and the strings play repeated pizzicato chords beneath it, following the soloist’s tempo. The score marks the clarinet lento, lungo (slowly, at length), then accelerando.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 32, rehearsal F: Moderato assai, Recitativo; clarinet ad libitum, lento lungo, accelerando; strings pizzicato and colla parte. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fanfare for muted trumpet and trombone
cues.text: The sharp fanfare for muted trumpet and trombone first sounds in this movement. Rimsky-Korsakov wrote that it returns in the finale “in the delineation of the wrecking ship”, though that episode has no connection with the Kalender’s tale.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, pp. 247–248. A muted trumpet (con sord.) begins the fanfare before rehearsal E in the full score, printed p. 30. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf ; https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

cues.title: Bassoon cadenza and final section
cues.text: The bassoon returns with a cadenza, following the earlier clarinet cadenza. Its tune opens the last large section of the movement. The same short figures are now accompanied by the brass march.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the two cadenzas, first clarinet and then bassoon, with the bassoon initiating the final section. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing Animato and B major chord
cues.text: Short woodwind phrases lead into the last page, marked Animato. Strings play rapid figures beneath brass chords, and timpani reinforce the bass. The B minor tale ends on a sharp B major chord.
cues.evidence: Full score, closing pages, especially printed p. 53: Animato and final B-major chord. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Violin cadenza to bassoon Andantino
transitions.to: A · Bassoon solo over muted double basses
transitions.how: The violin cadenza slows, marked ritardando assai. At the Andantino the bassoon begins its B minor tune above four muted double basses.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 25, end of the violin cadenza and opening Andantino. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The Sultan’s phrase becomes a march
transitions.from: A · Bassoon solo over muted double basses
transitions.how: A figure first played pizzicato by the low strings is taken up by the brass as fanfares. The figure is related to the Sultan’s motto, which connects this interruption to the first movement. Horns, trumpets and trombones exchange short calls over sustained chords in the woodwind and strings.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 30–31; Serotsky describes the low-string origin and the Sultan-motto connection. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm

transitions.title: Pizzicato strings under solo clarinet
transitions.how: The orchestral chord stops at a fermata. At Moderato assai (rehearsal F), a solo clarinet plays a free recitative. The strings play short repeated pizzicato chords marked colla parte, slowing and speeding up with the soloist.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 32, rehearsal F: clarinet solo and pizzicato strings marked colla parte. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, II, full-score scan
source.locator: Printed pp. 24–26: violin, bassoon and oboe solos; pp. 30–32: brass march and clarinet recitative with pizzicato strings; pp. 48–53: final return and B-major ending.

timeline.note: The solo violin plays above harp chords.
The bassoon begins above four muted double basses; harp and the violin’s held ending sound at the join.
The oboe takes the tune, with bassoon, horn and strings beneath it.
The strings take up the bassoon’s tune, with woodwinds joining its phrases.
Horns, trumpets and trombones exchange short fanfares above sustained strings and winds.
The clarinet plays freely above repeated pizzicato chords in the strings.
Piccolo, brass, timpani, triangle and cymbals join the strings as the march grows louder.
The bassoon plays the opening tune again above quiet strings.
Winds and strings broaden the tune, reinforced by brass and percussion.
Short woodwind phrases enter as the orchestral accompaniment thins.
At Animato, strings play fast under brass chords; timpani and cymbals reinforce the B-major ending.

composer.epithet: Russian composer known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
